Fundamentals of Tokenization and Semantic Partitioning for Systems with Generative AI and RAGs
In recent years, research in artificial intelligence applied to Natural Language Processing (NLP) has advanced exponentially, enabling innovative approaches for analyzing and interpreting large volumes of text. Techniques such as tokenization and semantic partitioning (or chunking) are essential for modern systems to handle extensive texts while maintaining context and semantic coherence. These methods become especially relevant in Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) architectures, which combine large language models (LLMs) with external information retrieval to enhance the quality of responses and reduce issues such as hallucinations. This article aims to discuss and present common strategies for tokenization and semantic partitioning of texts, showing how these processes allow grouping tokens into semantically coherent units, thereby feeding RAG systems with more accurate and contextualized data.
TOKENS AND TOKENIZATION:
Tokenization is the process of splitting a text into smaller units, called tokens. These tokens can represent words, subwords, or even characters, depending on the method used, and are crucial for language models to process and interpret the content. Below are some tokenization strategies:
I. Word-based Tokenization: In this method, each word is considered a token. For example, the sentence “I like apples” would be split into tokens: [“I”, “like”, “apples”]. This approach is simple but may struggle to handle compound words or morphological variations.
II. Subword-based Tokenization: Modern techniques such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) and WordPiece use statistical or probabilistic methods to split words into subunits. For example, the word “Multifunctional” could be split into: . This strategy is useful for handling rare or new words, as it allows the model to recognize common parts present in different terms.
III. Character-based Tokenization: In this method, each character is treated as a token. For example, the word “apple” would be split into: [“a”, “p”, “p”, “l”, “e”]. Although this is a highly granular approach, it can generate long token sequences, impacting processing efficiency.
IV. Space-based Tokenization: Some techniques use spaces as delimiters to define tokens. For instance, the sentence “Hello, world!” could be initially tokenized as: [“Hello,”, “world!”]. However, this simple method may not handle punctuation and special characters properly, requiring additional preprocessing to separate punctuation marks or handle specific cases.
Practical Example: Consider the following text as the basis for segmentations throughout the article:
Introduction: The Hobbit, written by J.R.R. Tolkien, is a fantasy novel first published in 1937. The story follows the journey of Bilbo Baggins, a hobbit who finds himself unexpectedly involved in an adventure with a group of dwarves and the wizard Gandalf. The narrative is rich in detail and presents a fascinating world filled with magical creatures and epic challenges.
Story: The adventure begins when Bilbo Baggins is approached by Gandalf and the dwarves, who invite him to join them on a mission to recover the treasure guarded by the dragon Smaug. The group faces various challenges, including trolls, goblins, and wargs, as they travel through Middle-earth. Bilbo ultimately confronts the dragon and manages to steal part of the treasure, but Smaug becomes furious and sets off in search of revenge. The story culminates in a great battle between dwarves, elves, men, and evil creatures, where Bilbo plays a crucial role.
Characters: Bilbo Baggins is the protagonist, a hobbit who transforms from someone averse to adventures into a brave hero. Gandalf is the wise wizard who guides Bilbo and the dwarves on their journey. Thorin Oakenshield is the leader of the dwarves, determined to reclaim his home and treasure. Smaug is the dragon who guards the dwarves’ treasure and represents a great danger.
Villains: The trolls are creatures that capture Bilbo and the dwarves but are defeated by Gandalf. The goblins are inhabitants of the Misty Mountains who capture Bilbo and his friends. The wargs are giant wolves that attack the group on several occasions. Smaug is the primary antagonist, whose greed and fury threaten all of Middle-earth.
Conclusion: The Hobbit is a masterpiece of fantasy literature that not only introduces readers to the world of Middle-earth but also explores themes of courage, friendship, and the battle between good and evil. Bilbo Baggins’ journey is a testament to personal growth and the discovery that even the most unlikely heroes can make a difference.
The tokenization stage is fundamental for semantic partitioning. These tokens serve as the foundation for organizing information into groups that share similar meanings or contexts, thus facilitating the process of semantic partitioning.
SEMANTIC PARTITIONING AND CREATION OF CHUNKS
When dealing with large documents, simply inputting the full text into a large language model (LLM) can be ineffective and costly, as well as increase the risk of hallucinations. To mitigate these issues, semantic partitioning is used, which is the process of splitting the text into smaller units, called chunks, that preserve the meaning and context of the original content. This strategy allows for the extraction of only the relevant parts of a document, facilitating search and improving the accuracy of responses. Additionally, by transforming each chunk into a vector representation (embedding), more efficient semantic searches can be conducted within RAG systems. Below, we describe some methods of semantic partitioning:
I. Fixed Size Chunking:
This technique divides the text into fixed-size units, usually measured in tokens or characters. For example, one might define chunks of 300 characters, with a slight overlap between segments to preserve context.
How the text is divided: The text is segmented into blocks based on a predefined limit (e.g., 300 characters).
How the chunk size is measured: It is usually calculated based on the character or token count, considering the input limits of LLMs.
II. Recursive Chunking:
This approach segments the content hierarchically, using delimiters that respect the semantic structure of the text. The list of delimiters can include: ["
", " ", " "] or others that make sense in the context.
How the text is divided: Initially, the text is divided into paragraphs. If the sum of the characters from two combined paragraphs remains below the limit (e.g., 200 characters), they are grouped. If the combination exceeds the limit, the first paragraph is kept, and the second is subdivided into sentences, and if necessary, into characters.
How the chunk size is measured: The chunk is evaluated based on the character or token count, with the goal of preserving semantic coherence.
Note: While effective, this technique may sometimes break important semantic units; therefore, it is essential to implement strategies that ensure the integrity of the context.
III. Chunking by Document Type:
This method uses the inherent structure of different document formats, such as Markdown, LaTeX, HTML, or programming languages (Python, JavaScript, etc.), to guide the division of the text.
How it works: By recognizing structural elements such as titles, subtitles, lists, and paragraphs, the system segments the document in a way that preserves the hierarchy and semantics of the data.
Practical example: A Markdown document containing sections like “Introduction,” “Story,” “Characters,” “Villains,” and “Conclusion” can be automatically partitioned according to these markers, facilitating the extraction of relevant chunks.

IV. Semantic Chunk:
Semantic Chunking is a technique aimed at grouping fragments of text based on meaning and context, using embeddings, which are vector representations of words, phrases, or documents. The process involves the following steps:
I. Sentence Segmentation: The text is divided into smaller parts, which can later be grouped together. This segmentation can use a recursive approach or other methods.
II. Indexing: Each chunk is converted into a vector (embedding) and indexed in a high-dimensional vector space, making semantic comparisons easier.
III. Clustering: Using similarity algorithms, the system identifies which chunks have semantic proximity, grouping them based on relevance.
IV. Sentence Distance Calculation: The vector distance is calculated (for example, using cosine similarity) to determine how similar the embeddings of the chunks are.
V. Merging Groups: Semantically close chunks are combined to strengthen the cohesion of the content.
VI. Splitting Dissimilar Sentences: Sentences that do not show similarity are kept separate to ensure better semantic coherence.
V. Agentic Chunk:
The technique known as Agentic Chunk represents an advanced approach in which artificial intelligence agents (LLMs) are employed to determine relevant segmentation points based on context. This technique utilizes an in-depth analysis of propositions (statements or ideas extracted from the text) to dynamically group information. The process generally involves:
I. Evaluation of Propositions: The agent analyzes each proposition extracted from the text, assessing its clarity and relevance using NLP techniques.
II. Topic Grouping: Based on semantic similarity algorithms, the propositions are grouped into related topics, using embeddings to compare their meanings.
III. Dynamic Adjustment: As new propositions are identified, the agent reevaluates existing groups, incorporating new information or creating new topics as needed.
This approach not only improves accuracy in text segmentation but also enhances the user experience by offering an organization of information that reflects the context and relevance of the extracted data.

Integration with RAG Systems
In Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, the stages of tokenization, semantic partitioning, and embedding generation are integrated to optimize information retrieval and response generation. The pipeline can be summarized as follows:
I. Tokenization: The text is converted into tokens, ensuring that the model understands the basic units of language.
II. Chunking/Semantic Partitioning: The document is divided into semantically coherent chunks to facilitate processing.
III. Indexing with Embeddings: Each chunk is transformed into a representative vector and stored in a vector index.
IV. Retrieval and Generation: When a query is made, the system retrieves the most relevant chunks by comparing embeddings and uses them to generate a response coherent with the context of the question.
This approach not only allows for the retrieval of relevant data but also the generation of responses that align with the original text’s context, reducing the risk of hallucinations and increasing the accuracy of the information returned.
Conclusion:
The evolution of artificial intelligence and NLP studies has led to significant advances in the analysis and interpretation of large volumes of text. Techniques such as tokenization and semantic partitioning are essential for building RAG systems, allowing large language models to access and process information accurately and contextually. By breaking texts into smaller and semantically coherent units, we can not only reduce the processing load but also improve the quality and relevance of the generated responses. Thus, the proper integration of these processes is a crucial step in enhancing information retrieval and generation systems.
